en: Clashing and thrusting,
I shall stand beside you.
Let me see the measure
Of that swine Sarybay!
You were a hero, you were a lion,
A warrior who knew the enemy’s ways.
Level your spear and break their ranks;
In fury, drive the enemy away!
Your heroic father is beside you—
Now unleash true slaughter!
Sarybay, who has challenged us,
Has shown his enmity thus.
Do not spare your precious life,
Do not glance to either side.
Level your spear and thrust it home,
Drive your spear in till it drips with blood,
Pierce both his eyes!
That swaggering brute,
That thick-armed would-be wrestler,
Has raised this great commotion from the start.
Rip open his belly like a donkey’s!
Choose your opening and thrust without wavering,
Drive it home before he can flinch,
Twist the spear in openly,
Watch him closely and strike!
Tear the flesh from the shins
Of that raging swine.
Keep clear of the crush and thrust,
Face him without fear and thrust!
Let dust rise where your spear strikes,
Let blood gush where your fist falls,
Let life flow mingled with the blood!
Let the true spear reach its mark,
And let not a scrap of the swine remain—
Let them all be ground to dust!
Thrust with unblinking eyes,
Gather all your wisdom and strength,
And at that gaudy swine
Strike swiftly till he topples.
Aim carefully and thrust,
Aim for the place that brings death.
Choose his flank and thrust;
Strike surely, not as he does.
Let me see the grievous wrath
Of that swaggering swine.
You have fought many times
Against that strong-armed swine;
My heroic son Külchoro,
Let me stand as your support.
Do not look around you;
This world is vain and deceitful—
Spare not your life at all!
Do not consider what is precious;
Spare not even your threadlike life!
Charge, my son, charge!” he cried,
“Give that fearsome swine
No chance to flee—finish him!
No man escapes his destined death,
No one turns back from dying.
Unleash a fierce battle,
Until not a hair’s breadth remains whole,
And slaughter one another.
Such is the harshness of battle.
Charge, my son, charge!” he cried,
“Seize that swine
Whom the whole world could not overcome!
Beat out his fury in earnest
And settle the final reckoning!
Grapple and wrench each other,
And test yourselves in combat.
Single out the forces
In which the swine places his trust;
Learn the measure of their courage,
And slice their bellies like fat.
Turn the river from its course,
And until you die in battle,
Slaughter the swine who came himself
As though fire had swept over him.
Smash him into dust,
Bathe the sword in blood,
And strike down all around him.
Beat out completely the rage
Of the wrathful boar—
Such is the nature of battle.
Let me see his prowess;
I came seeking you,
To grapple with him and spill his blood.”
His voice was heard, though he was unseen.
When he heard this news,
Choro, son of Almambet, said,
“That is my father’s voice,”
His heart filled with burning grief.
In the blink of an eye,
This wretched world passes away.
His father Almambet
Came riding forth from among the host.
From the side of the noonday sun,
All the forty companions,
With elder Kyrgyl at their head,
Appeared as though slaughter had struck,
Like arrows fiercely loosed,
As though returning to dwell among men,
As though they would drive and devour
All the world.
Renowned among the renowned were those heroes,
Illustrious, fierce-eyed champions,
Red-speared lions
Who had subdued the whole world
With their might.
While the lion Manas lived,
The forty companions were highly honored;
“Companion” was a formidable word—
Not forty companions, but forty comrades.
Each of the forty followed a different path,
All forty had broad white blazes,
Each of the forty had a different nature,
Each grim champion could shatter an age.
Words lose worth when said too often;
Among the forty companions,
There were all kinds, lacking none:
Some were so fierce that water could not penetrate them,
And there were heroic companions
Of gentle nature and open countenance.
There were also harsh companions,
Hot-tempered and abrupt.
There were heroic companions
Who never retreated from battle,
Never shrank a hair’s breadth from death,
Who turned their chargers’ heads
And stood beneath the banner.
There were clumsy companions
Who could not speak and had no words,
Who had chests but no substance,
Black heads and forked legs,
Human only in name,
Mere creatures born into the world.
There were cowardly companions
Who never stepped outside at night
And never uncovered their heads in sleep.
There were clumsy companions
Whose mottled flanks trembled.
All forty bore forty spears,
With curved swords at their belts,
And truly raised an uproar.
Now the spirits of the forty companions,
The heroic companions, brave Seytek,
And Kuyaly, daughter of Kayypchaal—
These warriors joined
The three as comrades.
Every side thundered,
With an uproar that split the sky,
As they joined them in companionship.
Looking toward this side,
One wore a blue silk coat.
His form loomed like a mountain,
His surge like a rushing river,
His bulk like a great elephant,
And such was his splendor.
His spear was steel, his arrow finely wrought,
His deeds were famed throughout the world.
The finest of the yellow-gray,
The most skillful of mountain game,
A fierce champion of the Kyrgyz,
He too was one of the precious few.
He was Chubak, son of Khan Balta,
With piercing shouts and ringing cries,
Another of the bloodthirsty warriors.
With a brass spear and mottled-headed mace,
In the echoing empty ravine,
He raised a piercing shout.
Chubak, son of Akbalta,
Also emerged from one side
And joined the rallying cry.
He strode proudly in his coat of mail.
When mortal men
Beheld him, their minds reeled.
A prince among humankind,
Choice among many lions,
The finest of living souls,
Perfect in wisdom and strong in might,
He leveled all who grappled with him.
Those who faced and leveled spears at him
Saw their age brought to ruin.
Those who crossed blades with him
Were uprooted entirely.
His lionheartedness was renowned;
When word of his wrath was heard,
Chylaba, khan of the Khakhan,
Wondered how he could wage war,
And the lord of the Black Chinese
Despaired of his dear life.
He raised piercing cries and tumult,
Bringing strife upon all he encountered.
Chubak, son of Khan Balta,
Appeared just as in life
And joined them as a comrade,
Raising a mighty shout.
He became a companion to Kuyaly, mighty Külchoro,
And gray-maned Seytek,
Joining all three.
Their opponent was Sarybay,
A fierce enemy such as this.
A dreadful and oppressive deed arose,
All who confronted him were leveled,
His weapons numbered eighty-four,
And wherever he advanced became fire.
In their battle frenzy, the heroes
Loaded these three:
A heavy matchlock, a musket, and a long gun.
The black earth did not overturn,
But halted beneath their multitude.
Their adversary was Sarybay,
A calamitous enemy such as this.
The gray-maned heroes were filled with ancestral spirit;
At the sight, the mind reeled.
Lofty in form, their eyes were embers,
They loomed like high blue mountains;
When the fierce champions moved,
They seemed able to conquer every age.
When the lions grew angry,
They seemed able to drive down and swallow
Not only Sarybay, but the entire world.
Such were their form and appearance.
Their majesty was great, their wrath was strong;
They loomed like that towering mountain.
Warriors mighty in wrestling,
Heroes who knew the enemy’s ways,
The three stayed united and did not scatter.
Against the infidel son Sarybay,
Not sparing their threadlike lives,
They began their fury in earnest.
That precious life needed divine favor;
The fierce champions, without the least regard,
Bound it by a thread and cast it aside.
They shouldered their fine, sturdy long guns,
Their jezails upon them,
And prayed to the Creator.
Invoking Babedin, they gave their blessing,
And vowed a moon-hoofed horse
To the forty saints and Kydyr for Kyyaz.
The heroic companions and brave Seytek
Still dwelt in Talas.
The lineage of Manas was not yet spent;
May they not break and scatter the banner,
Nor turn the eyes of the surging lion’s descendants
Toward the torments of hell.
Do not turn the ravine ridge into their road;
Do not let the princely children of Manas
Be disgraced by the wrathful.
When the time comes for their road to open,
They will destroy the hostile enemy,
When God grants the hour,
And it was said their destiny would be
Like the stars in the sky.
